question: Does stress change the risk or course of cancer? Answer factor by factor with the measured effect, and cite your sources (title, year, URL).
answer:
Stress does not act as one single factor in cancer. Measured effects differ by outcome:

**1. Work stress and getting cancer (incidence) - no measurable increase**
Meta-analysis of 12 European prospective cohorts, 116,000 men and women, 5,700 incident cancers:
Work stress vs. no work stress for all cancers combined: HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.90-1.04. No association for colorectal, lung, breast or prostate cancers.
Source: Work stress and risk of cancer: meta-analysis of 5700 incident cancer events in 116,000 European men and women, 2013, https://www.bmj.com/content/346/bmj.f165

**2. Broad psychosocial stress and getting cancer (incidence) - very small increase**
Meta-analysis of 165 observational studies in initially healthy people:
Stress-related psychosocial factors vs. none: HR 1.11 for cancer incidence, HR 1.29 for cancer mortality.
Source: Do stress-related psychosocial factors contribute to cancer incidence and survival?, 2008, https://www.nature.com/articles/ncponc1134

**3. Depression / chronic distress and dying from cancer - ~25% higher mortality**
Meta-analysis of 26 prospective studies in cancer patients, depression predicts:
Mortality RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.12-1.40 after adjustment; also predicts faster disease progression.
Source: Depression as a predictor of disease progression and mortality in cancer patients: a meta-analysis, 2009, https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cncr.24561

**4. Social isolation and survival after breast cancer - ~66% higher all-cause mortality**
Prospective Nurses' Health Study, 2,835 women with breast cancer:
Socially isolated vs. socially integrated: HR 1.66 for all-cause mortality and HR 2.14 for breast-cancer mortality.
Source: Social networks, social support, and survival after breast cancer diagnosis, 2006, https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2005.04.2846

**5. Experimental chronic stress and tumor growth - 2-3x larger tumors in animals**
Mouse orthotopic model of ovarian carcinoma, chronic restraint stress vs. no stress:
Increased tumor weight and number of nodules, increased VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, via beta-adrenergic activation. Propranolol blocked the effect.
Source: Chronic stress promotes tumor growth and angiogenesis in a mouse model of ovarian carcinoma, 2006, https://www.nature.com/articles/nm1447

**6. Blocking stress hormones and human cancer course - lower breast cancer mortality**
Population-based Irish cohort, 6,279 women with breast cancer:
Propranolol users vs. non-users: HR 0.19, 95% CI 0.06-0.60 for breast cancer-specific mortality.
Source: Beta blockers and breast cancer mortality: a population-based study, 2011, https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2010.33.5422

In short: everyday work stress alone does not measurably raise overall cancer incidence, but chronic distress, depression and social isolation are associated with modestly worse incidence, progression and mortality, and stress hormones can accelerate tumor biology in experimental models.
